name: Reselling business
blurb: Buy secondhand clothes and goods cheaply, then resell them online for more
title: Reselling Business: How to Resell Clothes Online
description: How a reselling business works, where to source and sell secondhand clothes and goods, what you need, the counterfeit risk and how to test with what you own.
h1: How to start a reselling business
answer: A reselling business buys secondhand clothes and goods from thrift stores, charity shops, garage sales, auctions or clearance, then lists them on online marketplaces for more than they cost. You earn the gap after platform fees, shipping and your time. The catch is that profit depends on knowing what is worth buying, every item needs photos and a listing, and counterfeit brand goods can get your account banned.

body: Each item is a small trade: you buy it below what buyers will pay online, clean it, photograph it, list it and ship it. Marketplaces take a selling fee and sometimes a payment fee, and you pay for packaging and, on some platforms, shipping.

Margins come from knowledge: recognising brands, materials, vintage pieces and sizes that sell, and avoiding items that will sit for months. Your time per item, from sourcing to posting, is the hidden cost.

ul: Accounts on one or two secondhand marketplaces that suit what you sell.
A small sourcing budget; many people start by selling things they already own.
A phone camera, a plain background, good light and a tape measure for clothing.
A habit of checking sold prices before buying, not asking prices.

Local paperwork: rules differ by country. Regular reselling for profit is usually taxable trading income, and marketplaces may report seller income to tax authorities. In the US, marketplaces must collect and verify identity and bank details from high-volume sellers of new or unused items under the INFORM Consumers Act.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People who enjoy thrifting and know brands or vintage
Anyone without space to store stock
Organised listers who like photos and descriptions
People who want a scalable business without hiring help
Someone who can start small with their own items
Anyone tempted to buy cheap "designer" goods without proof

ul: Counterfeits: selling fakes, even unknowingly, can bring account bans, refunds and legal trouble. Learn to authenticate brands you sell, or avoid them.
Dead stock: items that do not sell tie up cash and space.
Platform fee and policy changes that shift who pays fees or shipping.
Returns and disputes, including buyers claiming an item was not as described.
Sourcing "mystery boxes" or liquidation pallets sold as easy money often contain unsellable items.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: List ten items you already own and no longer need.
Before pricing, search sold listings for the same or similar items.
Track how long each item takes to sell and what you keep after fees and shipping.
Visit two or three thrift stores and note which items you could buy below recent sold prices.
Spend a small, fixed sourcing budget and see whether it returns a profit within a month or two.
Pick one or two categories you know, such as denim, outdoor gear or vintage tops.
Set up a photo corner and a standard listing template with measurements and flaws.
List consistently, a few items every day.
Keep a simple sheet of cost, sale price, fees and days to sell per item.
Register as a business and set aside tax once reselling becomes regular.

faq.q: What sells best when reselling clothes online?
faq.a: It depends on your market and platform. Recognised brands in good condition, quality materials and genuine vintage tend to sell more reliably than fast-fashion basics. Always check recently sold prices for your area before buying.

faq.q: Do I have to pay tax on reselling?
faq.a: Selling your own used belongings at a loss is often not taxed, but buying items to resell for profit usually counts as trading income. Rules differ by country, so check with your tax authority.

faq.q: How do I avoid selling fakes?
faq.a: Buy branded items only when you can check labels, materials, stitching and serial details against reliable references, and skip anything you cannot verify. Some marketplaces offer authentication for high-value items.
